title: Bonds
concept: A bond is generally a loan made by an investor to a company or government. The borrower promises interest payments and repayment under agreed terms.
learningObjective: Understand that buying a bond generally means lending money to an organisation rather than purchasing ownership in it.
primaryMisconception: Bonds are the same as stocks.
secondaryMisconceptions: Buying a bond gives the investor ownership or control of the borrower.
Bonds are completely risk-free and always repay investors on time.
keyTakeaway: Buying a bond generally means lending money, not owning the borrower.

screens.title: Owner or Lender?
screens.content: A company needs £10,000 but refuses to sell ownership. Investors still provide the money. What do they receive instead?
screens.illustration: A company stands between an ownership-share card and a loan agreement. The ownership card is crossed out.

screens.title: New Equipment Needed
screens.content: BrightBuild needs £10,000 for new equipment. Its owners want to keep ownership of the company.
screens.illustration: A workshop displays new equipment with a £10,000 price tag while the founders protect an ownership chart.

screens.title: Borrowing From Investors
screens.content: BrightBuild offers bonds to investors. Each bond includes rules about interest payments and when the borrowed money should be repaid.
screens.illustration: Several bond documents travel from the company to investors while money moves towards the company.

screens.title: Two Different Roles
screens.content: A shareholder owns part of a company. A bond investor lends money and receives a repayment promise instead of ownership.
screens.illustration: One path shows a shareholder ownership badge. The other shows a lender agreement and repayment calendar.

screens.title: What Does the Bond Investor Become?
screens.question: When you buy a company bond, what role do you generally take?

options.response: Correct. The company borrows your money and agrees to follow the bond’s repayment terms.
Ownership usually comes from shares. A bond generally creates a lending relationship instead.
Buying a bond does not normally give control over daily business decisions.
The investor provides money to the company but does not personally purchase or own its equipment.

screens.title: Ownership or Lending?
screens.instruction: Match each financial term with what it represents.

educationalAssumptions: BrightBuild and its bond are fictional.
The bond terms are simplified classroom examples.
A bond is generally a lending arrangement rather than company ownership.
Bond issuers may be companies, governments, or other organisations.
Interest and repayment are promises under the bond terms, not guaranteed outcomes.
A bond’s market value may rise or fall before its repayment date.
Real bonds can have different payment schedules, risks, prices, and conditions.
The activity does not recommend buying any real bond or stock.

rightSideItems.label: Money lent to a company or government
A possible distribution of company profits to shareholders
An amount paid to a lender for borrowing money

correctPairs.explanation: Buying stock generally makes the investor a partial owner. The stock’s value may rise or fall, and profit is not guaranteed.
Buying a bond generally means lending money to the issuer under agreed repayment and interest terms.
Some companies may distribute part of their profits to shareholders. Dividends are not guaranteed.
Interest is the amount the borrower agrees to pay for using the lender’s money.

incorrectMatchFeedback.feedback: A stock usually represents ownership. Lending money to an organisation is more closely connected with a bond.
A dividend may be paid to a shareholder, but the stock itself represents ownership.
Interest is generally paid to a lender. A shareholder may instead receive a dividend, although dividends are not guaranteed.
A bond generally makes the investor a lender, not a company owner.
Dividends are connected with shares and company ownership. Bonds may make interest payments under their terms.
Interest is a payment connected with a bond, but the bond itself represents the money lent.
A dividend is a possible payment to shareholders rather than the original money lent.
Both may provide income, but dividends come from company decisions while bond interest follows the bond’s agreed terms.
Receiving interest does not normally create company ownership.
Interest is paid for borrowing money. A dividend is a possible distribution to shareholders.

followUpQuestions.question: What does the investor own after buying this bond?

options.text: A lending claim under the bond agreement

followUpQuestions.explanation: The investor has lent £100 under agreed terms. The bond does not normally provide company ownership.

followUpQuestions.question: If BrightBuild makes every promised payment, how much would the investor receive over three years?
followUpQuestions.explanation: The investor receives three £4 interest payments, totalling £12, plus the £100 repayment.

followUpQuestions.question: Is receiving the full £112 guaranteed?

options.text: No, the borrower may struggle to make payments
No, because bonds never repay investors

followUpQuestions.explanation: The issuer promises to pay, but financial problems could cause delayed, reduced, or missed payments.

bondRiskReminder.explanation: The issuer may struggle to make interest payments or repay the borrowed amount.
The bond’s market value may rise or fall if it is sold before repayment.
Changes in wider interest rates may affect the bond’s market value.
Future payments may buy less if prices rise.

placementRules: Each term must be matched with one meaning.
Each meaning may be used once.
There is one correct definition for each term.
Matches may be completed in any order.
All three follow-up questions must be answered correctly.

screens.title: Lending Instead of Owning
screens.content: You matched a bond with money lent to a company or government. Buying a bond generally makes you a lender, not an owner. The issuer promises interest payments and repayment under agreed terms. A stock represents ownership and may provide dividends, while a bond creates a repayment claim. Bonds may sometimes move less sharply than some stocks, but they are not risk-free. Payments can be missed, and the bond’s market value can change.
screens.simpleSummary: Stocks create ownership; bonds generally create a lending relationship.
screens.illustration: A stock certificate connects to an ownership badge, while a bond connects to a lending agreement and payment calendar.

screens.title: Funding a School Project
screens.content: A fictional organisation needs £500 for equipment. Instead of selling ownership, it issues five £100 bonds. Investors lend the money and expect interest plus repayment under the agreement. They do not own the organisation, and payment problems are still possible.
screens.illustration: Five £100 bond cards fund one equipment purchase while ownership remains unchanged.

questions.text: Which situation describes buying a bond?

options.text: Lending money to an organisation under agreed terms
options.feedback: Correct. A bond generally represents money lent to an issuer.

options.text: Buying partial ownership in a company
options.feedback: Partial ownership is generally represented by stock rather than a bond.
Buying a product makes someone a customer, not a bond investor.
Bond payments depend on the issuer meeting its obligations and are not guaranteed profits.

questions.correctExplanation: A bond generally represents money lent to an issuer, which promises interest and repayment according to the agreement.
questions.misconceptionTested: Buying a bond creates company ownership.

questions.text: Which statement correctly compares stocks and bonds?

options.text: Stocks generally represent ownership; bonds generally represent lending
options.feedback: Correct. Shareholders are owners, while bondholders are generally lenders.
They may both be investments, but they create different financial relationships.
Stocks can fall in value, and bond issuers can miss payments.

options.text: Bonds always give more control than stocks
options.feedback: Bondholders are generally lenders and do not normally control company decisions.

questions.correctExplanation: A shareholder owns part of a company. A bond investor generally lends money to an issuer under agreed terms.
questions.misconceptionTested: Bonds are the same as stocks.

questions.text: A company bond promises repayment next year, but the company develops serious financial problems. What should the investor understand?

options.text: The company may delay or miss payments
options.feedback: Correct. The repayment promise remains, but the company may be unable to fulfil it.
A promise to repay does not remove the possibility that the issuer may struggle financially.

options.text: The investor now owns the company
options.feedback: Payment difficulties do not turn a bondholder into a shareholder.
A bond’s market value may rise or fall before repayment, especially when the issuer’s financial condition changes.

questions.correctExplanation: A bond creates a repayment promise, but the issuer may be unable to fulfil every payment.
questions.misconceptionTested: Bonds are completely risk-free and always repay investors on time.

reviewChecklist.notes: The mission focuses on bonds as lending arrangements rather than company ownership.
The mission distinguishes principal repayment, interest, bondholder claims, shareholders, dividends, default risk, and changing bond values.
The mission uses a fictional equipment purchase, a £100 classroom bond, simple calculations, and introductory investment terms.
The mission does not recommend any real company, government, bond, stock, or investment decision.
The mission clearly states that promised bond payments may be delayed, reduced, or missed.
The mission contains no predictions involving real stocks, bonds, companies, or markets.
Borrowers, lenders, shareholders, missed payments, and investment losses are discussed neutrally.
The mission includes repayment risk, market-price risk, interest-rate risk, inflation risk, and different real-world bond terms.
The mission uses pounds, companies, equipment purchases, school projects, lending agreements, and familiar UK financial language.
The learner directly matches bonds with lending, stocks with ownership, interest with lenders, and dividends with shareholders.
The quiz addresses bonds versus stocks, ownership, control, repayment promises, and bond risks.

reviewChecklist.item: Mission can be completed in under five minutes
reviewChecklist.notes: The mission uses three short story screens, four matching pairs, three follow-up questions, and three concise quiz questions.

reviewChecklist.item: Language matches the target reading level
reviewChecklist.notes: The language is clear, practical, respectful, and appropriate for teens aged 13–17.
